title: Numbers and telling the time
goal: Count up to the millions with a system that makes complete sense, and read Norwegian clock times — including one "half" that works the opposite way to British English.
bekal: say the numbers 0 to 1,000,000 and prices in kroner
tell the time with *halv*, *kvart over* and *kvart på*
name the days, months and dates
wave: Go back over **Unit 4** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the dialogue. Look at every noun — what gender is it, and what's its ending?

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På Oslo S
dialogs.intro: Oslo Central Station, in the morning. Budi is standing in front of a flickering departures board, not sure what he's looking at.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Unnskyld, når går toget til Trondheim?
lines.id: Excuse me, when does the train to Trondheim leave?
lines.literal: excuse, when goes the-train to Trondheim?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Klokka sju førti. Om ti minutter.
lines.literal: the-clock seven forty. in ten minutes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Oh no. And the next one?

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Ja, nettopp. Halv ni betyr tretti minutter før ni.
lines.id: Yes, exactly. *Halv ni* means thirty minutes before nine.
lines.literal: yes, exactly. half nine means thirty minutes before nine.

lines.speaker: Lars:
lines.text: Fire hundre og nitti kroner. Men på lørdag koster den halvparten.
lines.id: Four hundred and ninety kroner. But on Saturday it's half price.
lines.literal: four hundred and ninety kroner. but on Saturday costs it the-half-part.

notes: **This is the trap almost every English speaker falls into: *halv ni* means 8:30, not 9:30.** Norwegian counts **toward** the next hour — "half (on the way to) nine". British English *half nine* means the exact opposite, 9:30. Burn this into your memory now; missed trains and meetings start right here.

**Klokka sju førti** — clock times are said just as they're written, like reading a digital display. For official timetables (trains, planes, cinemas), Norwegians use the 24-hour clock: *klokka nitten førti* for 19:40.
**Om ti minutter** = "in ten minutes", looking ahead. It came up in Unit 3 and will keep coming up; its partner is *for ti minutter siden* = "ten minutes ago".

**Fire hundre og nitti** — notice the *og* in the middle of the number. Norwegian inserts "and" between the hundreds and the rest, just like British English: 490 = "four hundred **and** ninety". The *og* here is just a quick **oh**.
**Kroner** is abbreviated **kr** and written after the number: *490 kr*. One krone is divided into a hundred *øre*, but *øre* has practically vanished — prices are always rounded to the krone.

grammars.title: Numbers 0 to 20
body: These twenty-one words are the only part you have to learn by heart. After that, everything can be assembled.
after: ⚠️ **Seksten is pronounced SAIS-ten**, not "sex-ten". The *k* disappears and the *e* becomes *ai*. It's the only number that really lies about its spelling.
⚠️ **Sytten is pronounced SÖT-ten** and **tjue is pronounced HYÜ-eh** — the combination *tj-* sounds the same as *kj-*: the soft hiss of the *h* in "huge".
The number **7** has two forms, both correct: *sju* (more modern, more common in speech) and *syv* (older, still frequent in writing). Use *sju*.

grammars.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands
body: From 21 on, modern Norwegian builds numbers **from big to small**, just like English: *tjueen* = "twenty-one".
after: ⚠️ **An old system can still be heard from older people:** *enogtyve* for 21, literally "one-and-twenty" — the small number first, just like German and Danish (and old-fashioned English "four-and-twenty blackbirds"). It was officially dropped in 1951, but phone numbers and birth years are sometimes still said that way. **Just recognize it; use the new system.**

Norwegian uses a dot (or a space) to separate thousands and a comma for decimals — the exact opposite of English: *1.500,50 kr* is one thousand five hundred kroner and fifty øre. Watch out for this on price tags and receipts.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Norwegian uses *klokka* to talk about the time. The official form uses the numbers as they are; the conversational form uses quarters and halves.
after: **Over** means "past", **på** means "to", **kvart** means "quarter", and **halv** points to the **next** hour. These four words cover the whole system.

The 8:25 and 8:35 rows look excessive to an English ear, but Norwegians really use them — they measure from *halv*, not from the full hour. If it feels too complicated, the official form (*åtte tjuefem*) can always be used and is never wrong.

blocks.text: **Days and months are written with a small letter** in Norwegian — unlike English. *mandag*, not *Mandag*.

The *-dag* ending on the days always shrinks to **-dah** in speech; nobody really pronounces the *g*. And *tirsdag*, *torsdag*, *onsdag* contain the combinations *rs* and *ns*, which have a hissing sound — listen more than once before you imitate.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Read aloud: 17, 27, 70, 76, 116, 490, 1500 and 2026. If one of them trips you up, it's most likely *sytten*, *seksten* or *tjue* — the three numbers whose sound is furthest from their spelling.
Look at the time now and say it in two forms: conversational and official. Repeat every time you check the time today.
Say your full date of birth, including the year. It's a question you'll really be asked at the immigration office, the bank and the doctor's.

Put the words in the right order.
